fields.definition: The process of detecting and removing unwanted non-musical mouth sounds—lip smacks, clicks, saliva crackles, and tongue noises—from a recorded vocal track using specialized de-click/de-crackle tools or manual waveform editing.
fields.plain_english: This means cleaning small mouth sounds out of a singer's recording. Lip smacks, clicks, and spit noises get removed, so only the words are left. It is like wiping smudges off a photo to make the picture look clean.
fields.purpose_function: It removes distracting mouth sounds that become obvious once a vocal is compressed and pushed to the front of a mix, keeping the listener's focus on the words and tone.
fields.practical_application: An engineer zooms into the waveform between words and uses a mouth de-click module or short fades to silence tiny clicks, usually before compression exaggerates them.
common_mistakes: Removing so many mouth sounds that the vocal sounds unnatural and lifeless
Confusing sibilance (ess sounds) with mouth clicks and treating them the same way
Cutting whole sections instead of just the click, leaving audible gaps in room tone
scenario_contexts: Cleaning a close-mic'd lead vocal before heavy compression in a pop mix
Preparing an intimate acoustic ballad where every mouth noise is audible
Editing a voiceover or podcast where clicks distract from the message

sources: iZotope RX technical documentation (Mouth De-click / De-click)

fields.definition: The reduction of excessive low-midrange energy in a vocal, typically in the range of roughly 150–500 Hz, usually with EQ cuts, to remove a boomy, cluttered "muddy" quality and improve clarity.
fields.plain_english: This means turning down the thick, boomy lower part of a voice. Too much energy around 200 to 400 Hz makes a voice sound muffled. Cutting it a little makes the words clearer, like opening a window in a stuffy room.
fields.purpose_function: It clears low-mid buildup so the vocal sits clearly in the mix and does not clash with bass, guitars, and other instruments crowding the same range.
fields.practical_application: The engineer sweeps a narrow EQ boost to find the boomy frequency, then cuts a few dB there, often around 200–400 Hz, while listening to the vocal in the full mix.
common_mistakes: Cutting too much low-mid so the vocal becomes thin and weak
Judging mud on the soloed vocal instead of in the full mix where it matters
Setting a high-pass filter too high and losing the natural body of the voice
scenario_contexts: Cleaning up a male lead vocal that sounds boomy on a dense rock track
Fixing a proximity-effect buildup from a singer working close to the mic
Making room for bass and rhythm guitar in a crowded arrangement

sources: Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio (Mike Senior)

fields.definition: A dynamics process that splits a vocal signal into separate frequency bands and compresses each independently, allowing problem ranges such as boomy lows or harsh highs to be controlled without affecting the whole signal.
fields.plain_english: This tool splits the voice into low, middle, and high parts, then controls the loudness of each part on its own. So you can calm just the boomy or harsh part without changing the rest. It is like having a separate volume knob for each part of the sound.
fields.purpose_function: It tames only the frequency ranges that jump out—like a boom on low notes or a harsh edge on loud words—so the vocal stays even without dulling the whole track.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sets a band around the harsh or boomy range and applies gentle compression there, tightening trouble spots while leaving the rest of the vocal untouched.
common_mistakes: Over-compressing every band until the vocal sounds squashed and lifeless
Using it to fix problems that a simple EQ cut would solve more cleanly
Setting crossover points carelessly and creating an uneven, phasey tone
scenario_contexts: Controlling a singer whose low notes boom while high notes stay fine
Smoothing an uneven vocal recorded with inconsistent mic distance
Taming harsh loud words on a bright vocal during vocal processing

fields.definition: The reduction of an excessively nasal, honky quality in a vocal, typically by cutting a narrow band in the roughly 1–2 kHz region with EQ or dynamic EQ, where nasal resonance tends to concentrate.
fields.plain_english: This means fixing a voice that sounds too honky, like someone talking through their nose. The problem sits around 1000 to 2000 Hz. Cutting a little there makes the voice sound more open and natural.
fields.purpose_function: It removes a pinched, nasal tone that can make a vocal sound unpleasant, helping the voice sound fuller and more natural in the mix.
fields.practical_application: The engineer sweeps a narrow EQ cut through the low treble to find the honky spot, then reduces it a few dB, sometimes with a dynamic EQ so it acts only on the nasal notes.
common_mistakes: Cutting too wide a band and making the vocal sound dull and distant
Confusing natural vocal formants with a nasal problem and over-correcting
Removing so much that the vocal loses presence and intelligibility
scenario_contexts: Fixing a singer with a naturally nasal tone on a lead vocal
Reducing honk caused by a mic or room emphasizing the low treble
Cleaning up backing vocals that sound pinched when stacked

sources: Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio (Mike Senior)

fields.definition: The timing adjustment of the start (onset) of vocal notes or phrases—especially across doubled or stacked takes—so their attacks begin together, tightening the ensemble and cleaning up the stereo image.
fields.plain_english: This means lining up the exact moment each vocal take starts. When you stack two takes, their first sounds should hit at the same time. If they do not, you nudge them so they start together, like two hands clapping as one.
fields.purpose_function: It makes doubled and layered vocals sound tight and unified instead of loose or flammed, which is vital when several takes share the same words.
fields.practical_application: The engineer zooms into the waveform starts and slides syllables earlier or later so a double lines up with the lead, or uses timing-alignment software to match them.
common_mistakes: Aligning so perfectly that stacked vocals lose their natural width and thickness
Lining up only the note starts while ignoring where the words end
Creating clicks or gaps when moving syllables without crossfading the edits
scenario_contexts: Tightening a doubled chorus vocal against the lead take
Lining up a group of stacked backing vocals singing the same line
Fixing a late entrance where a singer came in slightly behind the beat

sources: Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio (Mike Senior)

fields.definition: A technique in which a heavily compressed copy of a vocal is blended underneath the original, largely uncompressed track, adding density and sustain while preserving natural dynamics and transients; also called New York or parallel compression.
fields.plain_english: This means mixing a squashed copy of the voice under the normal one. The squashed copy fills in the quiet parts, while the main track keeps its punch. It is like putting a soft cushion under the voice so nothing gets lost.
fields.purpose_function: It raises the quieter details and adds body and consistency to a vocal without crushing the loud peaks, keeping the performance lively yet steady.
fields.practical_application: The engineer sends the vocal to a bus with strong compression, then blends that bus quietly beneath the main vocal, adjusting the balance to taste.
common_mistakes: Blending in too much compressed signal so the vocal sounds pumping and unnatural
Forgetting to match latency and causing phase problems between the two tracks
Using it as a substitute for fixing a poorly recorded or badly performed take
scenario_contexts: Adding sustain and body to a lead vocal in a pop or R&B mix
Bringing up quiet breaths and word tails on an intimate vocal
Giving a thin backing vocal more weight without obvious compression

fields.definition: Fast-acting compression applied to a vocal to catch and reduce short, loud transient peaks, evening out the level so the vocal stays controlled and can be brought forward in the mix safely.
fields.plain_english: This means catching the loudest quick spikes in a voice and turning them down. Singers often jump loud on certain words, and this smooths those jumps. It is like a quick hand on the volume knob for every loud burst.
fields.purpose_function: It controls sudden loud peaks so the vocal has a steadier level, stopping spikes from clipping or jumping out and letting the overall vocal sit louder in the mix.
fields.practical_application: The engineer uses a fast attack and moderate ratio to clamp peaks, watching the gain-reduction meter so only the loudest moments are tamed.
common_mistakes: Setting the attack too fast and dulling the natural consonants and life of the vocal
Using a high ratio that squashes the whole vocal instead of just the peaks
Chasing meters instead of listening for when the compression sounds natural
scenario_contexts: Taming loud belted notes in a dynamic pop lead vocal
Controlling peaks before a vocal reaches a limiter or further processing
Evening out a singer who moves a lot on and off the mic

fields.definition: Editing a vocal at the level of whole phrases or lines—cutting, moving, timing, cleaning, and crossfading them—to assemble and polish a performance, as opposed to editing single syllables or the whole track at once.
fields.plain_english: This means working on a voice one line or phrase at a time. You cut, move, fix timing, and clean up each phrase, then smooth the joins. It is like editing a story sentence by sentence instead of all at once.
fields.purpose_function: It lets an engineer shape and repair a vocal performance in manageable chunks, fixing timing and cleaning gaps while keeping the natural flow of each line.
fields.practical_application: The engineer splits the vocal into phrases, nudges or replaces weak lines, trims noise between them, and crossfades the edits so the joins are inaudible.
common_mistakes: Leaving hard edits with no crossfade, causing clicks at the joins
Cutting room tone or breaths unevenly so phrases sound disconnected
Over-editing until the performance loses its natural feel
scenario_contexts: Assembling a final lead vocal from several takes phrase by phrase
Fixing the timing of a single weak line in an otherwise good take
Cleaning noise and breaths between sung phrases before mixing

sources: Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio (Mike Senior)

fields.definition: Replacing a specific phrase, word, or line in a vocal track with the same phrase from another take or a re-recorded punch-in, matching level, timing, and tone so the swap is seamless.
fields.plain_english: This means swapping one bad line in a vocal for a better version of the same line. You take the good phrase from another take and drop it in. It is like fixing one wrong word in a sentence without rewriting the whole page.
fields.purpose_function: It fixes a single flawed phrase—wrong pitch, poor timing, or a slip—without redoing the whole vocal, saving the good parts of a performance.
fields.practical_application: The engineer finds a better take of the problem line, drops it onto the timeline, matches its timing and level, and crossfades the edges so the replacement blends in.
common_mistakes: Using a replacement phrase whose tone or mic distance does not match the rest
Forgetting to align the timing so the swapped line feels off
Leaving an audible level or room-tone jump at the edit points
scenario_contexts: Swapping a flat-pitched word for a better take in a lead vocal
Punching in a corrected line the singer re-recorded later
Replacing a mistimed phrase during vocal comping

sources: Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio (Mike Senior)
